To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the UK electricity industry represents the domestic electricity customer as a ‘deficit model’ of human behaviour, which limits the potential for systemic energy change.
the electricity supply industry in the UK is dominated by a deficit model of human behavior, which is not likely to change as a result of current government policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how the electricity industry represents the demand side, and to what extent these representations are likely to change as a result of increased deployment of domestic-scale renewable energy technologies.
the ways in which the electricity industry represents the electricity customer and how these representations may evolve as a result of increased renewable energy deployment.
the ways in which the UK electricity supply sector represents domestic electricity consumers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UK electricity industry is not yet prepared for the challenges associated with a more participatory approach to domestic electricity demand.
the electricity industry is not yet prepared for a significant role for domestic electricity users as energy prosumers.

, although the UK electricity supply system has been restructured to facilitate the deployment of renewable energy, the dominant representation of domestic consumers within that system remains as passive, unengaged and ignorant of energy matters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that a majority of electricity supply industry stakeholders represent the human behaviour in a 'deficit' manner as either a lack of information or appropriate technologies.
the current UK electricity industry is not well equipped to deal with the challenges of domestic-scale renewable energy.
the UK electricity industry is currently not well placed to respond to the opportunities and challenges presented by domestic renewable energy deployment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to develop more sophisticated representations of the domestic electricity user in order to facilitate the transition to a low carbon energy system.
the electricity industry is not yet prepared to engage with the public in a meaningful dialogue about the future of energy systems and the role of the public as active participants in energy systems.
the current regulatory and institutional environment in the UK is not conducive to a more participatory and sustainable approach to domestic-scale renewable energy technologies.
